title: Ziba or Mephibosheth — whose account of the day David fled was true?
summary: When David flees Jerusalem, Ziba tells him that Mephibosheth has stayed behind expecting to be given “the kingdom of my father”, and David gives Ziba all that was Mephibosheth’s. When David returns, Mephibosheth says “my servant deceived me” and that Ziba “hath slandered thy servant”. David answers, “Thou and Ziba divide the land.” The verses compared do not say which of the two accounts was true.
text: KJV 2 Samuel 9:9: “I have given unto thy master's son all that pertained to Saul and to all his house.” KJV 9:10: “Thou therefore, and thy sons, and thy servants, shall till the land for him” KJV 9:13: “So Mephibosheth dwelt in Jerusalem”; “and was lame on both his feet” KJV 4:4: “that he fell, and became lame” KJV 16:1: “behold, Ziba the servant of Mephibosheth met him, with a couple of asses saddled” KJV 16:2: “The asses be for the king's household to ride on” KJV 16:3: “And the king said, And where is thy master's son? And Ziba said unto the king, Behold, he abideth at Jerusalem: for he said, To day shall the house of Israel restore me the kingdom of my father.” KJV 16:4: “Then said the king to Ziba, Behold, thine are all that pertained unto Mephibosheth.” KJV 19:17: “and Ziba the servant of the house of Saul, and his fifteen sons and his twenty servants with him; and they went over Jordan before the king” KJV 19:24: “And Mephibosheth the son of Saul came down to meet the king, and had neither dressed his feet, nor trimmed his beard, nor washed his clothes, from the day the king departed until the day he came again in peace.” KJV 19:25: “Wherefore wentest not thou with me, Mephibosheth?” KJV 19:26: “And he answered, My lord, O king, my servant deceived me: for thy servant said, I will saddle me an ass, that I may ride thereon, and go to the king; because thy servant is lame.” KJV 19:27: “And he hath slandered thy servant unto my lord the king; but my lord the king is as an angel of God: do therefore what is good in thine eyes.” KJV 19:29: “And the king said unto him, Why speakest thou any more of thy matters? The narrator does add one statement in its own voice: Mephibosheth “had neither dressed his feet, nor trimmed his beard, nor washed his clothes, from the day the king departed until the day he came again in peace” (19:24). title: “again the anger of the Lord was kindled against Israel” — for what, before David numbered the people?
summary: The chapter opens with the Lord’s anger already kindled “against Israel”, before describing David being moved to number the people. Seventy thousand die. David says the sin is his and asks of the people, “these sheep, what have they done?” The verses compared name no act of Israel that the anger was for, and do not say to what earlier anger “again” looks back.

Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 2 Samuel 24:1: Καὶ προσέθετο ὀργὴν Κύριος ἐκκαῆναι ἐν Ἰσραήλ, καὶ ἐπέσεισε τὸν Δαυὶδ ἐν αὐτοῖς [and the Lord added wrath to burn in Israel, and stirred up David among them]. 1 Chronicles 21:1: Καὶ ἔστη διάβολος ἐν τῷ Ἰσραήλ [and a slanderer, or the devil, stood in Israel]. reasoning: In the order of 24:1 the anger comes first and the numbering second: the anger is “against Israel”, and David is moved “against them”. title: “But he lied unto him” — why did the old prophet of Bethel lie to the man of God?
summary: An old prophet of Bethel tells the man of God from Judah that an angel has ordered him to bring him home to eat, and the narrator adds “But he lied unto him.” The man of God eats, is sentenced by the word of the Lord spoken through the same old prophet, and is killed by a lion. The verses read state the lie and its result; they do not state why the old prophet told it.
text: KJV 1 Kings 13:9: “For so was it charged me by the word of the Lord, saying, Eat no bread, nor drink water, nor turn again by the same way that thou camest.” KJV 13:11: “Now there dwelt an old prophet in Bethel; and his sons came and told him all the works that the man of God had done that day in Bethel” KJV 13:15: “Then he said unto him, Come home with me, and eat bread.” KJV 13:18: “He said unto him, I am a prophet also as thou art; and an angel spake unto me by the word of the Lord, saying, Bring him back with thee into thine house, that he may eat bread and drink water. But he lied unto him.” KJV 13:19: “So he went back with him, and did eat bread in his house, and drank water.” KJV 13:20: “And it came to pass, as they sat at the table, that the word of the Lord came unto the prophet that brought him back:” KJV 13:21: “Forasmuch as thou hast disobeyed the mouth of the Lord” KJV 13:22: “thy carcase shall not come unto the sepulchre of thy fathers.” KJV 13:24: “And when he was gone, a lion met him by the way, and slew him” KJV 13:26: “It is the man of God, who was disobedient unto the word of the Lord” KJV 13:30: “And he laid his carcase in his own grave; and they mourned over him, saying, Alas, my brother!” KJV 13:31: “When I am dead, then bury me in the sepulchre wherein the man of God is buried; lay my bones beside his bones” KJV 13:32: “For the saying which he cried by the word of the Lord against the altar in Bethel” … “shall surely come to pass.” KJV 2 Kings 23:18: “And he said, Let him alone; let no man move his bones. So they let his bones alone, with the bones of the prophet that came out of Samaria.” Hebrew (WLC) 1 Kings 13:18: וּמַלְאָ֡ךְ דִּבֶּ֣ר אֵלַי֩ בִּדְבַ֨ר יְהוָ֜ה [and an angel spoke to me by the word of the Lord] … כִּחֵ֖שׁ לֹֽו [he lied to him]. 13:31: אֵ֚צֶל עַצְמֹתָ֔יו הַנִּ֖יחוּ אֶת־עַצְמֹתָֽי [beside his bones lay my bones]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 1 Kings 13:18: καὶ ἐψεύσατο αὐτῷ [and he lied to him]. 13:31: παρὰ τὰ ὀστᾶ αὐτοῦ θέτε με, ἵνα σωθῶσι τὰ ὀστᾶ μου μετὰ τῶν ὀστῶν αὐτοῦ [lay me beside his bones, that my bones may be preserved with his bones]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/11/13/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/1KI13.htm.
reasoning: The chapter states a good deal about the old prophet. His sons told him what the man of God had done and said (13:11); he rode after him and invited him home (13:15); when refused, he claimed an angel’s command, and the narrator says in the same verse that this was a lie (13:18). The word of the Lord then came to that same prophet at the table, and he spoke the sentence (13:20–22). After the death he said the man “was disobedient unto the word of the Lord” (13:26), buried him in his own grave, mourned “Alas, my brother!”, asked to be buried beside him, and affirmed that the saying against the altar “shall surely come to pass” (13:30–32). What none of these verses gives is the reason for the lie. The gap matters to the passage: the man of God had been charged to eat no bread there (13:9), he had refused the same invitation once (13:16–17), the lie is the stated means by which he was brought back, and his death follows from it.
scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. Readings that have been proposed, none of which the verses quoted state: that the old prophet wished to test whether the man of God would keep his charge; that he wanted the company or the honour of a man whose word had just been confirmed by a sign; that he acted for Bethel and its altar, to undo or discredit the message; that he sought a tie with the man of God for his own sake, in the light of his later request to lie in the same grave. Limits: the narrator’s words fix that the claim of an angel was a lie and do not describe the speaker’s purpose; the chapter records no reproof of the old prophet in the verses read, and that is not evidence of how the act was judged; the sentence at 13:21–22 is addressed to the man of God and names his own disobedience as its ground. The Greek of 13:31 has the added words “that my bones may be preserved with his bones”: that states a purpose for the burial request, not for the lie, and 2 Kings 23:18 reports that both sets of bones were left alone. title: Elijah is told to anoint Hazael, Jehu and Elisha — did Elijah anoint any of them?
summary: At Horeb the Lord tells Elijah to anoint Hazael king over Syria, Jehu king over Israel and Elisha prophet in his place. In the verses read, Elijah casts his mantle on Elisha; it is Elisha who tells Hazael he will be king; and a young prophet sent by Elisha pours oil on Jehu. The verses read report no anointing done by Elijah, and they do not say how the command given to him was carried out.
text: KJV 1 Kings 19:15: “And the Lord said unto him, Go, return on thy way to the wilderness of Damascus: and when thou comest, anoint Hazael to be king over Syria:” KJV 19:16: “And Jehu the son of Nimshi shalt thou anoint to be king over Israel: and Elisha the son of Shaphat of Abelmeholah shalt thou anoint to be prophet in thy room.” KJV 19:19: “and Elijah passed by him, and cast his mantle upon him.” KJV 19:21: “Then he arose, and went after Elijah, and ministered unto him.” KJV 2 Kings 2:13: “He took up also the mantle of Elijah that fell from him” KJV 2 Kings 8:13: “And Elisha answered, The Lord hath shewed me that thou shalt be king over Syria.” KJV 2 Kings 8:15: “and Hazael reigned in his stead.” KJV 2 Kings 9:1: “And Elisha the prophet called one of the children of the prophets, and said unto him, Gird up thy loins, and take this box of oil in thine hand, and go to Ramothgilead” KJV 2 Kings 9:3: “Then take the box of oil, and pour it on his head, and say, Thus saith the Lord, I have anointed thee king over Israel.” KJV 2 Kings 9:6: “and he poured the oil on his head, and said unto him, Thus saith the Lord God of Israel, I have anointed thee king over the people of the Lord, even over Israel.” KJV 2 Chronicles 22:7: “Jehu the son of Nimshi, whom the Lord had anointed to cut off the house of Ahab.” Hebrew (WLC) 1 Kings 19:15: וּבָ֗אתָ וּמָשַׁחְתָּ֧ אֶת־חֲזָאֵ֛ל לְמֶ֖לֶךְ עַל־אֲרָֽם [and you shall come and anoint Hazael as king over Aram]. 19:16: תִּמְשַׁ֥ח לְמֶ֖לֶךְ עַל־יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל [you shall anoint as king over Israel] … תִּמְשַׁ֥ח לְנָבִ֖יא תַּחְתֶּֽיךָ [you shall anoint as prophet in your place]. 19:19: וַיַּשְׁלֵ֥ךְ אַדַּרְתֹּ֖ו אֵלָֽיו [and he cast his mantle to him]. 2 Kings 9:6: וַיִּצֹ֥ק הַשֶּׁ֖מֶן אֶל־רֹאשֹׁ֑ו [and he poured the oil on his head]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 1 Kings 19:15: καὶ ἥξεις καὶ χρίσεις τὸν Ἀζαὴλ εἰς βασιλέα τῆς Συρίας [and you shall come and anoint Azael to be king of Syria]. 19:16: χρίσεις εἰς προφήτην ἀντὶ σοῦ [you shall anoint to be prophet in your place]. 19:19: καὶ ἐπέῥῥιψε τὴν μηλωτὴν αὐτοῦ ἐπʼ αὐτόν [and he cast his mantle upon him]. 2 Kings 8:13: ἔδειξέ μοι Κύριός σε βασιλεύοντα ἐπὶ Συρίαν [the Lord has shown me you reigning over Syria]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/11/19/, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/12/9/, https://ebible.org/grcbrent/1KI19.htm and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/2KI08.htm.
reasoning: The command is in the second person and names three acts for Elijah: “anoint Hazael”, Jehu “shalt thou anoint”, Elisha “shalt thou anoint”. The verses read report something for each of the three men. Elijah finds Elisha and casts his mantle on him, and Elisha follows and serves him (19:19–21); the verse names a mantle and does not name oil or use the word “anoint”. With Hazael it is Elisha who speaks, at Damascus, and his words are that the Lord has shown him that Hazael will be king (2 Kings 8:13); no oil and no word “anoint” stands in 8:7–15. Jehu is anointed with oil, by “one of the children of the prophets” whom Elisha sends (2 Kings 9:1–6). The command lists Hazael, Jehu and Elisha, while the account presents Elisha, Hazael and Jehu. The list does not explicitly require that the acts occur in its stated order. The gap matters because the command is the Lord’s answer to Elijah at Horeb and sets out what is to follow; the verses read do not say whether Elijah did any of the three acts himself, or by what step the task passed to Elisha.
scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. Readings that have been proposed, none of which the verses quoted state: that Elijah carried out the command through his successor, so that what Elisha did or ordered counts as done by Elijah; that “anoint” is used here for appointing or designating, so that the mantle and the spoken word answer to it; that Elijah did anoint one or more of the three in acts the books do not report; that the command was left in part undone by Elijah. Limits: the command sets no time and does not say that Elijah must act in person at each step; that an act is not reported does not show that it was not done; 2 Chronicles 22:7 says the Lord had anointed Jehu and names no human hand; the casting of the mantle is not called an anointing in the verses read, and it is not said there to be anything else. title: Twelve pieces, ten tribes and “one tribe” — which tribe is the twelfth?
summary: Ahijah tears a garment into twelve pieces, gives Jeroboam ten for “ten tribes”, and says Solomon’s son shall have “one tribe”. Ten and one make eleven. In the KJV and the Hebrew, the verses read do not say whose the twelfth piece is or which tribe it stands for; Brenton’s Greek reads “two tribes” at 11:32 and 11:36.
text: KJV 1 Kings 11:13: “Howbeit I will not rend away all the kingdom; but will give one tribe to thy son” KJV 11:30: “And Ahijah caught the new garment that was on him, and rent it in twelve pieces:” KJV 11:31: “And he said to Jeroboam, Take thee ten pieces: for thus saith the Lord, the God of Israel, Behold, I will rend the kingdom out of the hand of Solomon, and will give ten tribes to thee:” KJV 11:32: “But he shall have one tribe for my servant” KJV 11:35: “But I will take the kingdom out of his son's hand, and will give it unto thee, even ten tribes.” KJV 11:36: “And unto his son will I give one tribe” KJV 12:20: “there was none that followed the house of David, but the tribe of Judah only.” KJV 12:21: “he assembled all the house of Judah, with the tribe of Benjamin” KJV 12:23: “unto all the house of Judah and Benjamin, and to the remnant of the people” KJV 2 Chronicles 11:12: “having Judah and Benjamin on his side.” KJV Joshua 19:1: “and their inheritance was within the inheritance of the children of Judah.” Hebrew (WLC) 1 Kings 11:30: שְׁנֵ֥ים עָשָׂ֖ר קְרָעִֽים [twelve pieces]. 11:31: וְנָתַתִּ֣י לְךָ֔ אֵ֖ת עֲשָׂרָ֥ה הַשְּׁבָטִֽים [and I will give you the ten tribes]. 11:32: וְהַשֵּׁ֥בֶט הָאֶחָ֖ד יִֽהְיֶה־לֹּ֑ו [and the one tribe shall be his]. 11:36: וְלִבְנֹ֖ו אֶתֵּ֣ן שֵֽׁבֶט־אֶחָ֑ד [and to his son I will give one tribe]. 12:20: זוּלָתִ֥י שֵֽׁבֶט־יְהוּדָ֖ה לְבַדֹּֽו [except the tribe of Judah alone]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 1 Kings 11:13: σκῆπτρον ἓν δώσω τῷ υἱῷ σου [one tribe I will give to your son]. 11:30: δώδεκα ῥήγματα [twelve pieces]. 11:31: καὶ δώσω σοι δέκα σκῆπτρα [and I will give you ten tribes]. 11:32: Καὶ δύο σκῆπτρα ἔσονται αὐτῷ [and two tribes shall be his]. 11:36: Τῷ δὲ υἱῷ αὐτοῦ δώσω τὰ δύο σκῆπτρα [and to his son I will give the two tribes]. 12:20: πάρεξ σκήπτρου Ἰούδα καὶ Βενιαμὶν μόνοι [except the tribe of Judah and Benjamin alone]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/11/11/, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/11/12/, https://ebible.org/grcbrent/1KI11.htm and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/1KI12.htm.
reasoning: The sign gives the numbers itself: twelve pieces (11:30), ten to Jeroboam for “ten tribes” (11:31, 11:35), and “one tribe” for Solomon’s line (11:13, 11:32, 11:36). The prophet does not say what becomes of the two remaining pieces, and the sum of the tribes named is eleven. The account that follows says first that none followed the house of David “but the tribe of Judah only” (12:20) and in the next verse that Rehoboam gathered “all the house of Judah, with the tribe of Benjamin” (12:21). So in the KJV and the Hebrew quoted, the verses read leave open which tribe the twelfth piece stands for and on which side it is counted. The gap matters because the sign is the stated ground of the division of the kingdom, and the count is its content. The Greek quoted does give a count that reaches twelve at two of the verses: it has “two tribes” at 11:32 and 11:36 and “Judah and Benjamin” at 12:20, while at 11:13 it has “one tribe”, as the Hebrew does.
scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. Readings that have been proposed, none of which the KJV and Hebrew verses quoted state: that the twelfth tribe is Benjamin, held with Judah by Rehoboam (12:21, 12:23; 2 Chronicles 11:12), and that “one tribe” means one beside Judah, David’s own; that “one tribe” is Judah, with Benjamin or Simeon counted within it (Joshua 19:1 places Simeon’s inheritance inside Judah’s); that Levi, which had no territory of its own, is the tribe left out of the count; that “ten” and “one” are round figures for the greater part and the lesser. The Greek quoted states the count of two at 11:32 and 11:36; it does not name the two there, and it names Judah and Benjamin at 12:20. Limits: the sign does not say that every piece stands for one tribe on one side, though 11:31 ties ten pieces to ten tribes; a list of the twelve tribes is not given in these verses, and the Bible counts the tribes in more than one way, so which names make up the “ten” is not fixed by the verses read; 12:20 and 12:21 can both be true if Benjamin joined Rehoboam after the people made Jeroboam king, a step the text does not report; the Greek readings are wording differences stated here and not proposed as a separate finding. Those are word searches and a reading of the verses listed, not a reading of Kings and Chronicles in full. These checked verses, in the KJV and the Hebrew, do not say which tribe is the twelfth. title: “The book of the acts of Solomon” — what was this book, and is it the source Chronicles names?
summary: For the rest of Solomon’s acts and his wisdom, 1 Kings sends the reader to “the book of the acts of Solomon”. A phrase search of the packaged KJV finds that title in this verse only. At the same point 2 Chronicles names three other writings. The verses read do not say who wrote the book, what it held beyond the words quoted, or whether it is the same as any of the three.
text: KJV 1 Kings 11:41: “And the rest of the acts of Solomon, and all that he did, and his wisdom, are they not written in the book of the acts of Solomon?” KJV 1 Kings 14:19: “behold, they are written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel.” KJV 1 Kings 14:29: “are they not written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah?” KJV 2 Chronicles 9:29: “Now the rest of the acts of Solomon, first and last, are they not written in the book of Nathan the prophet, and in the prophecy of Ahijah the Shilonite, and in the visions of Iddo the seer against Jeroboam the son of Nebat?” Hebrew (WLC) 1 Kings 11:41: הֲלֹֽוא־הֵ֣ם כְּתֻבִ֔ים עַל־סֵ֖פֶר דִּבְרֵ֥י שְׁלֹמֹֽה [are they not written on the book of the words (or acts) of Solomon?]. 2 Chronicles 9:29: הֲלֹא־הֵ֣ם כְּתוּבִ֗ים עַל־דִּבְרֵי֙ נָתָ֣ן הַנָּבִ֔יא [are they not written on the words of Nathan the prophet]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 1 Kings 11:41: οὐκ ἰδοὺ ταῦτα γέγραπται ἐν βιβλίῳ ῥημάτων Σαλωμών; [behold, are not these written in a book of the words of Solomon?]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/11/11/, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/14/9/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/1KI11.htm.
reasoning: The verse names the book by a title and says what is in it: “the rest of the acts of Solomon, and all that he did, and his wisdom”. That much is stated. The verses read do not say who wrote it, when, or where it was kept, and the account of Solomon closes by pointing to it for what the account itself leaves out. From the next reign onward the same formula points to differently named books, “the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel” (14:19) and “of the kings of Judah” (14:29). At the matching place 2 Chronicles 9:29 points instead to “the book of Nathan the prophet”, “the prophecy of Ahijah the Shilonite” and “the visions of Iddo the seer”. The gap matters because the verse directs readers to another writing for additional information about Solomon, without explaining that writing’s identity or its relation to the sources named in Chronicles.
scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. Readings that have been proposed, none of which the verses quoted state: that the book was a record of Solomon’s reign kept at court, distinct from the later “chronicles of the kings”; that it is the same body of writing that 2 Chronicles 9:29 cites under the names of Nathan, Ahijah and Iddo; that it was a collection that held sayings as well as deeds, in view of “and his wisdom”; that it has not survived. Limits: the two books may point to different writings for the same reign without conflict, and no conflict is asserted here; that a title is found in one verse by a phrase search does not show that the writing is not meant elsewhere under another name; whether any existing writing is this book is not something these verses settle; the Hebrew word in the title can mean “words” or “acts”, and the KJV has “acts” for it in both halves of the verse. Check made: 1 Kings 11:41–43, 14:19 and 14:29 and 2 Chronicles 9:29 were read in the KJV, and 1 Kings 11:41 and 2 Chronicles 9:29 also in the Hebrew and 1 Kings 11:41 in the Greek; a phrase search of the packaged KJV for “acts of Solomon” finds 1 Kings 11:41 and 2 Chronicles 9:29, and for “book of the acts” finds 1 Kings 11:41 only. Those are phrase searches, not a reading of the whole Bible. These checked verses do not say who wrote the book of the acts of Solomon or whether it is one of the writings named at 2 Chronicles 9:29. title: “There was great indignation against Israel” — whose indignation, and why did Israel depart?
summary: Israel, Judah and Edom are winning the war against Moab when the king of Moab offers his eldest son as a burnt offering on the wall. The next sentence says “there was great indignation against Israel”, and the armies go home. The verses read do not say whose indignation it was, why it fell on Israel, or how it made the armies leave.
text: KJV 2 Kings 3:18: “And this is but a light thing in the sight of the Lord: he will deliver the Moabites also into your hand.” KJV 3:24: “And when they came to the camp of Israel, the Israelites rose up and smote the Moabites, so that they fled before them: but they went forward smiting the Moabites, even in their country.” KJV 3:26: “And when the king of Moab saw that the battle was too sore for him, he took with him seven hundred men that drew swords, to break through even unto the king of Edom: but they could not.” KJV 3:27: “Then he took his eldest son that should have reigned in his stead, and offered him for a burnt offering upon the wall. summary: When Jehu has Joram’s body thrown into Naboth’s field, he recalls a word of the Lord about “the blood of Naboth, and the blood of his sons”. title: “The Lord gave Israel a saviour” — who was the saviour?
summary: In the account of Jehoahaz the narrator says that “the Lord gave Israel a saviour, so that they went out from under the hand of the Syrians”. The verse does not name him, and the same chapter says that Hazael oppressed Israel “all the days of Jehoahaz”. The verses read do not say who the saviour was or when he came.
text: KJV 2 Kings 13:3: “And the anger of the Lord was kindled against Israel, and he delivered them into the hand of Hazael king of Syria, and into the hand of Benhadad the son of Hazael, all their days.” KJV 13:4: “And Jehoahaz besought the Lord, and the Lord hearkened unto him: for he saw the oppression of Israel, because the king of Syria oppressed them.” KJV 13:5: “(And the Lord gave Israel a saviour, so that they went out from under the hand of the Syrians: and the children of Israel dwelt in their tents, as beforetime.” KJV 13:7: “Neither did he leave of the people to Jehoahaz but fifty horsemen, and ten chariots, and ten thousand footmen” KJV 13:22: “But Hazael king of Syria oppressed Israel all the days of Jehoahaz.” KJV 13:25: “And Jehoash the son of Jehoahaz took again out of the hand of Benhadad the son of Hazael the cities, which he had taken out of the hand of Jehoahaz his father by war. Three times did Joash beat him, and recovered the cities of Israel.” KJV 14:27: “but he saved them by the hand of Jeroboam the son of Joash.” Hebrew (WLC) 2 Kings 13:5: וַיִּתֵּ֨ן יְהוָ֤ה לְיִשְׂרָאֵל֙ מֹושִׁ֔יעַ [and the Lord gave to Israel a deliverer]. 14:27: וַיֹּ֣ושִׁיעֵ֔ם בְּיַ֖ד יָרָבְעָ֥ם בֶּן־יֹואָֽשׁ [and he delivered them by the hand of Jeroboam son of Joash]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 2 Kings 13:5: Καὶ ἔδωκε Κύριος σωτηρίαν τῷ Ἰσραὴλ [and the Lord gave deliverance to Israel]. 14:27: καὶ ἔσωσεν αὐτοὺς διὰ χειρὸς Ἱεροβοὰμ υἱοῦ Ἰωάς [and he saved them by the hand of Jeroboam son of Joas]. The verse stands inside the account of Jehoahaz, after his prayer (13:4), yet the chapter also says that the king of Syria left Jehoahaz almost no army (13:7) and that Hazael oppressed Israel “all the days of Jehoahaz” (13:22). title: “I have found the book of the law in the house of the Lord” — which book was it, and how had it gone out of knowledge?
summary: In Josiah’s eighteenth year the high priest says he has “found the book of the law in the house of the Lord”. The king hears it, rends his clothes and reforms Judah by it. The verses read call it the book of the law and the book of the covenant, and Chronicles calls it a book of the law of the Lord given by Moses; they do not say how much writing it held, where it had been, or how it came to be found at that time.

And Hilkiah gave the book to Shaphan, and he read it.” KJV 22:11: “And it came to pass, when the king had heard the words of the book of the law, that he rent his clothes.” KJV 22:13: “because our fathers have not hearkened unto the words of this book, to do according unto all that which is written concerning us.” KJV 23:2: “and he read in their ears all the words of the book of the covenant which was found in the house of the Lord.” KJV 23:21: “And the king commanded all the people, saying, Keep the passover unto the Lord your God, as it is written in the book of this covenant.” KJV 23:24: “that he might perform the words of the law which were written in the book that Hilkiah the priest found in the house of the Lord.” KJV 14:6: “according unto that which is written in the book of the law of Moses” KJV 2 Chronicles 34:14: “And when they brought out the money that was brought into the house of the Lord, Hilkiah the priest found a book of the law of the Lord given by Moses.” KJV Deuteronomy 31:26: “Take this book of the law, and put it in the side of the ark of the covenant of the Lord your God, that it may be there for a witness against thee.” Hebrew (WLC) 2 Kings 22:8: סֵ֧פֶר הַתֹּורָ֛ה מָצָ֖אתִי בְּבֵ֣ית יְהוָ֑ה [the book of the law I have found in the house of the Lord]. 23:2: סֵ֣פֶר הַבְּרִ֔ית הַנִּמְצָ֖א בְּבֵ֥ית יְהוָֽה [the book of the covenant that was found in the house of the Lord]. 2 Chronicles 34:14: סֵ֥פֶר תֹּֽורַת־יְהוָ֖ה בְּיַד־מֹשֶֽׁה [the book of the law of the Lord by the hand of Moses]. Deuteronomy 31:26: לָקֹ֗חַ אֵ֣ת סֵ֤פֶר הַתֹּורָה֙ הַזֶּ֔ה [take this book of the law]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 2 Kings 22:8: βιβλίον τοῦ νόμου εὗρον ἐν οἴκῳ Κυρίου [a book of the law I have found in the house of the Lord]. 23:2: τοῦ βιβλίου τῆς διαθήκης τοῦ εὑρεθέντος ἐν οἴκῳ Κυρίου [of the book of the covenant that was found in the house of the Lord]. 2 Chronicles 34:14: βιβλίον νόμου Κυρίου διὰ χειρὸς Μωυσῆ [a book of the law of the Lord by the hand of Moses]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/12/22/, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/12/23/, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/14/34/, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/5/31/, https://ebible.org/grcbrent/2KI22.htm, https://ebible.org/grcbrent/2KI23.htm and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/2CH34.htm.
reasoning: The verses read say several things about the book. It was found in the house of the Lord by Hilkiah (22:8; 23:24). It is called “the book of the law” (22:8, 22:11), “the book of the covenant” (23:2) and “the book of this covenant” (23:21), and Chronicles calls it “a book of the law of the Lord given by Moses” (2 Chronicles 34:14). title: Uz, Hul and Gether: sons of Shem, or sons of Aram?
summary: Chronicles lists Uz, Hul, Gether and Meshech in one run under “The sons of Shem”. Genesis gives Shem five sons and calls Uz, Hul, Gether and Mash “the children of Aram”. Brenton’s Greek of the Chronicles verse names only the first two sons of Shem and none of the four.

Hebrew (WLC) Genesis 10:23: וּבְנֵ֖י אֲרָ֑ם ע֥וּץ וְח֖וּל וְגֶ֥תֶר וָמַֽשׁ [and the sons of Aram: Uz and Hul and Gether and Mash]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 1 Chronicles 1:17, the whole verse as printed: Υἱοὶ Σὴμ, Αἰλὰμ, καὶ Ἀσσοὺρ, [sons of Sem: Ælam and Assur]. The cited page prints verse numbers 1 to 10, then 17, then 24 onward; it prints no verses 11 to 16 or 18 to 23. Verse 24 as printed begins: καὶ Ἀρφαξὰδ, Σάλα, [and Arphaxad, Sala]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) Genesis 10:23: Καὶ υἱοὶ Ἀρὰμ, Οὒζ, καὶ Οὒλ, καὶ Γατὲρ, καὶ Μοσόχ [and sons of Aram: Uz and Ul and Gater and Mosoch]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/13/1/, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/1/10/, https://ebible.org/grcbrent/1CH01.htm and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/GEN10.htm.
reasoning: In the KJV and the Hebrew of Chronicles nothing separates Aram from the four names that follow: all nine stand under “The sons of Shem”. Genesis ends Shem’s sons at Aram and gives the four to Aram. Brenton’s Greek of the Chronicles verse stops after the second name, so this verse has neither the four names nor Arphaxad, Lud and Aram; the next verse printed, 24, begins with Arphaxad.

The two KJV statements can stand together if “sons” in Chronicles takes in grandsons, or if the Chronicles list is a shortened copy of Genesis that leaves out the words “and the children of Aram”; the verse does not say either. title: Saul’s father Kish: son of Ner, or son of Abiel and brother of Ner?
summary: Chronicles says twice “Ner begat Kish, and Kish begat Saul”. Samuel calls Kish “the son of Abiel”, calls Ner “the son of Abiel”, with “Saul's uncle” in the description of Abner son of Ner. Chronicles 9:36 also lists a Kish and a Ner side by side as sons of one father.

title: In the ark: nothing “save the two tables”, or also the pot of manna and Aaron’s rod?

title: A source for Solomon’s acts: the visions of “Iddo the seer”, or of Joel?

title: Asa and Baasha: war “all their days”, or no war until Asa’s thirty-fifth year?
summary: Kings says twice that there was war between Asa and Baasha all their days, and starts Baasha’s reign in Asa’s third year. Chronicles says there was “no more war” until the thirty-fifth year of Asa’s reign, and then tells of Baasha’s attack in the thirty-sixth.

Hebrew (WLC) 2 Chronicles 15:19: וּמִלְחָמָ֖ה לֹ֣א הָיָ֑תָה עַ֛ד שְׁנַת־שְׁלֹשִׁ֥ים וְחָמֵ֖שׁ לְמַלְכ֥וּת אָסָֽא [and war there was not until the thirty-fifth year of the reign of Asa]. title: The men who killed Joash: sons of an Ammonitess and a Moabitess, or an Ammanite and a Moabite?

title: Ahaz’s burial: “with his fathers in the city of David”, or not brought “into the sepulchres of the kings”?
summary: Kings says Ahaz “was buried with his fathers in the city of David”. Chronicles says they buried him “in the city, even in Jerusalem: but they brought him not into the sepulchres of the kings of Israel”.
text: KJV 2 Kings 16:20: “And Ahaz slept with his fathers, and was buried with his fathers in the city of David” KJV 2 Chronicles 28:27: “And Ahaz slept with his fathers, and they buried him in the city, even in Jerusalem: but they brought him not into the sepulchres of the kings of Israel” Hebrew (WLC) 2 Kings 16:20: וַיִּקָּבֵ֥ר עִם־אֲבֹתָ֖יו בְּעִ֣יר דָּוִ֑ד [and he was buried with his fathers in the city of David]. 2 Chronicles 28:27: וַֽיִּקְבְּרֻ֤הוּ בָעִיר֙ בִּיר֣וּשָׁלִַ֔ם כִּ֚י לֹ֣א הֱבִיאֻ֔הוּ לְקִבְרֵ֖י מַלְכֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל [and they buried him in the city, in Jerusalem, for they did not bring him to the tombs of the kings of Israel]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 2 Chronicles 28:27: καὶ ἐτάφη ἐν πόλει Δαυὶδ, ὅτι οὐκ εἰσήνεγκαν αὐτὸν εἰς τοὺς τάφους τῶν βασιλέων Ἰσραὴλ [and he was buried in the city of David, for they did not bring him into the tombs of the kings of Israel]. 2 Kings 16:20: καὶ ἐτάφη ἐν πόλει Δαυὶδ [and he was buried in the city of David]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/12/16/, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/14/28/, https://ebible.org/grcbrent/2CH28.htm and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/2KI16.htm.
reasoning: Ahaz’s fathers were the kings of Judah. Kings places him with them in burial; Chronicles says he was not brought into the kings’ tombs.
scope: No tag is proposed. The KJV follows the Hebrew in each book. Brenton’s Greek of Chronicles has “in the city of David” where the KJV has “in the city, even in Jerusalem”, and Brenton’s Greek of the Kings verse does not print the words “with his fathers” after “was buried”; these are stated as wording and the Greek keeps the exclusion from the kings’ tombs. If “with his fathers” means only the same city and not the same tombs, the statements agree; Kings does not say so. The Hebrew quoted is the Westminster Leningrad Codex digital text. title: Manasseh’s altars in the house of the Lord: taken away by Manasseh, or beaten down by Josiah?
summary: Both books say Manasseh built altars in the two courts of the house of the Lord. Chronicles says that Manasseh himself later took away all the altars he had built there and cast them out of the city. Kings says that Josiah, two reigns later, beat down “the altars which Manasseh had made in the two courts of the house of the Lord”.
text: KJV 2 Chronicles 33:5: “And he built altars for all the host of heaven in the two courts of the house of the Lord.” KJV 2 Kings 21:5: “And he built altars for all the host of heaven in the two courts of the house of the Lord.” KJV 2 Chronicles 33:15: “And he took away the strange gods, and the idol out of the house of the Lord, and all the altars that he had built in the mount of the house of the Lord, and in Jerusalem, and cast them out of the city.” KJV 2 Kings 23:12: “and the altars which Manasseh had made in the two courts of the house of the Lord, did the king beat down” KJV 2 Chronicles 33:22: “for Amon sacrificed unto all the carved images which Manasseh his father had made, and served them” Hebrew (WLC) 2 Chronicles 33:15: וְכָל־הַֽמִּזְבְּחֹ֗ות אֲשֶׁ֥ר בָּנָ֛ה בְּהַ֥ר בֵּית־יְהוָ֖ה וּבִירוּשָׁלִָ֑ם וַיַּשְׁלֵ֖ךְ ח֥וּצָה לָעִֽיר [and all the altars that he had built in the mount of the house of the LORD and in Jerusalem, and he cast them outside the city]. Hebrew (WLC) 2 Kings 23:12: וְאֶת־הַֽמִּזְבְּחֹות֙ אֲשֶׁר־עָשָׂ֣ה מְנַשֶּׁ֔ה בִּשְׁתֵּ֛י חַצְרֹ֥ות בֵּית־יְהוָ֖ה נָתַ֣ץ הַמֶּ֑לֶךְ [and the altars that Manasseh had made in the two courts of the house of the LORD the king pulled down]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 2 Chronicles 33:15: καὶ πάντα τὰ θυσιαστήρια, ἃ ᾠκοδόμησεν ἐν ὄρει οἴκου Κυρίου καὶ ἐν Ἱερουσαλὴμ, καὶ ἔξωθεν τῆς πόλεως [and all the altars which he built in the mount of the house of the Lord and in Jerusalem and outside the city]. 2 Kings 23:12: καὶ τὰ θυσιαστήρια ἃ ἐποίησε Μανασσῆς ἐν ταῖς δυσὶν αὐλαῖς οἴκου Κυρίου καθεῖλεν ὁ βασιλεὺς [and the altars which Manasses made in the two courts of the house of the Lord the king pulled down]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/14/33/, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/12/23/, https://ebible.org/grcbrent/2CH33.htm and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/2KI23.htm.
reasoning: Chronicles has “all the altars that he had built in the mount of the house of the Lord” removed and thrown out of the city in Manasseh’s lifetime. Kings has altars that Manasseh made, in the courts of the same house, still standing for Josiah to break down.

The statements can both stand if the altars were set up again after Manasseh removed them, for example under Amon; 2 Chronicles 33:22 says that Amon sacrificed to the carved images his father had made, and no verse quoted reports altars being rebuilt. Brenton’s Greek of 33:15 as printed has no verb for casting out and reads “and outside the city” as a third place; that is stated as wording and no G is proposed on it here. title: Jehoiakim’s end: bound “to carry him to Babylon” — the Greek says he was carried there, and was buried with his fathers
summary: The KJV of Chronicles says Nebuchadnezzar bound Jehoiakim “to carry him to Babylon” and the quoted Chronicles verses do not describe his death or burial. Brenton’s Greek says the king “carried him away to Babylon”, and two verses later adds that Jehoiakim slept with his fathers “and was buried in Ganozae with his fathers”. Jeremiah had said he would have “the burial of an ass”, cast out beyond the gates.
text: KJV 2 Chronicles 36:6: “Against him came up Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, and bound him in fetters, to carry him to Babylon.” KJV 36:8: “Now the rest of the acts of Jehoiakim, and his abominations which he did, and that which was found in him, behold, they are written in the book of the kings of Israel and Judah: and Jehoiachin his son reigned in his stead.” KJV 2 Kings 24:6: “So Jehoiakim slept with his fathers: and Jehoiachin his son reigned in his stead.” KJV Jeremiah 22:19: “He shall be buried with the burial of an ass, drawn and cast forth beyond the gates of Jerusalem.” KJV Jeremiah 36:30: “and his dead body shall be cast out in the day to the heat, and in the night to the frost” Hebrew (WLC) 2 Chronicles 36:6: וַיַּֽאַסְרֵ֙הוּ֙ בַּֽנְחֻשְׁתַּ֔יִם לְהֹלִיכֹ֖ו בָּבֶֽלָה [and he bound him in bronze fetters to take him to Babylon]. 36:8 ends: עַל־סֵ֛פֶר מַלְכֵ֥י יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל וִֽיהוּדָ֑ה וַיִּמְלֹ֛ךְ יְהֹויָכִ֥ין בְּנֹ֖ו תַּחְתָּֽיו [in the book of the kings of Israel and Judah; and Jehoiachin his son reigned in his place]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 2 Chronicles 36:6: καὶ ἔδησεν αὐτὸν ἐν χαλκαῖς πέδαις, καὶ ἀπήγαγεν αὐτὸν εἰς Βαβυλῶνα [and bound him in bronze fetters, and carried him away to Babylon]. 36:8: καὶ ἐκοιμήθη Ἰωακὶμ μετὰ τῶν πατέρων αὐτοῦ, καὶ ἐτάφη ἐν γανοζαὴ μετὰ τὼν πατέρων αὐτοῦ, καὶ ἐβασίλευσεν Ἰεχονίας υἱὸς αὐτοῦ ἀντʼ αὐτοῦ [and Joakim slept with his fathers, and was buried in Ganozae with his fathers, and Jechonias his son reigned in his place]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) Jeremiah 22:19: Ταφὴν ὄνου ταφήσεται [he shall be buried with the burial of an ass]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/14/36/, https://ebible.org/grcbrent/2CH36.htm and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/JER22.htm.
reasoning: At 36:6 the KJV and the Hebrew state a purpose; the Greek states that it was done. At 36:8 the Greek has a death notice and a burial that the KJV and the Hebrew of the verse lack. The burial matters beside Jeremiah’s two sayings about Jehoiakim’s body: a burial “with his fathers” and “the burial of an ass … beyond the gates of Jerusalem” are different ends.
scope: G applies at 2 Chronicles 36:6 for “carried him away”, and at 36:8 for the added death and burial. The KJV states “slept with his fathers” in another book, at 2 Kings 24:6; it states no burial of Jehoiakim in any verse quoted here. The Jeremiah verses are sayings about what would happen, not reports that it happened, and the record does not claim that the Greek of Chronicles contradicts them: a body could be cast out and afterwards buried, and no verse quoted says so. The Greek of 36:8 names a burial place without explaining its location or how the burial relates to the journey to Babylon. These quotations alone do not establish a return from Babylon. The cited Greek page prints lettered verses 2a to 2c, 4a and 5a to 5d in this chapter; the wording quoted is printed at the plain numbers 6 and 8. Brenton’s Greek numbers Jeremiah 36 as chapter 43; only the KJV is quoted for Jeremiah 36:30. A separate published record deals with the words “none to sit upon the throne” in that verse. title: “There came a writing to him from Elijah the prophet” — when was it written, and how did it reach Jehoram?
summary: Jehoram of Judah receives a writing from Elijah that condemns him for killing his brothers, an act Chronicles places after his father Jehoshaphat’s death. Kings tells of Elijah being taken up into heaven before it tells of a campaign in which Jehoshaphat is still alive. The verses do not say when the writing was made or who carried it.
text: KJV 2 Chronicles 21:12: “And there came a writing to him from Elijah the prophet, saying, Thus saith the Lord God of David thy father, Because thou hast not walked in the ways of Jehoshaphat thy father, nor in the ways of Asa king of Judah,” KJV 21:13: “and also hast slain thy brethren of thy father's house, which were better than thyself” KJV 21:1: “Now Jehoshaphat slept with his fathers” KJV 21:4: “Now when Jehoram was risen up to the kingdom of his father, he strengthened himself, and slew all his brethren with the sword” KJV 2 Kings 2:11: “and Elijah went up by a whirlwind into heaven” KJV 2 Kings 3:11: “But Jehoshaphat said, Is there not here a prophet of the Lord” … “Here is Elisha the son of Shaphat, which poured water on the hands of Elijah” KJV 2 Kings 1:17: “And Jehoram reigned in his stead in the second year of Jehoram the son of Jehoshaphat king of Judah” KJV 2 Kings 8:16: “Jehoshaphat being then king of Judah” Hebrew (WLC) 2 Chronicles 21:12: וַיָּבֹ֤א אֵלָיו֙ מִכְתָּ֔ב מֵֽאֵלִיָּ֥הוּ הַנָּבִ֖יא לֵאמֹ֑ר [and there came to him a writing from Elijah the prophet, saying]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 2 Chronicles 21:12: Καὶ ἦλθεν αὐτῷ ἐν γραφῇ παρὰ Ἠλιοὺ τοῦ προφήτου, λέγων [and there came to him in writing from Eliu the prophet, saying]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/14/21/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/2CH21.htm.
reasoning: The writing speaks of the killing of Jehoram’s brothers as already done, and Chronicles tells that killing after Jehoshaphat’s death. Kings tells of Elijah’s going up in its second chapter, and in its third has Jehoshaphat alive and Elisha introduced as the man who “poured water on the hands of Elijah”. The timing affects how the event is read: the writing may have arrived during Elijah’s earthly life, or after his departure, including a writing composed beforehand and delivered later. The quoted verses do not settle these possibilities.
scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. Readings that have been proposed, none of which the quoted verses state: that Elijah was still on earth, the order of telling in Kings not being the order of events; that Jehoram had begun to reign while his father lived, as 2 Kings 1:17 and 8:16 may suggest, and the killings fall in that time; that Elijah wrote beforehand and the writing was delivered later; that the writing came from Elijah after he had been taken up; that another man of the name is meant. What the verses do state is that a writing came, that it was from Elijah the prophet, and what it said. The words “poured water on the hands of Elijah” describe Elisha’s past service and do not by themselves say that Elijah was gone. Check made: the eight verses quoted were read in the KJV, and 21:12 in the Hebrew and in Brenton’s Greek; a whole-word search of the packaged KJV for “Elijah” finds 2 Chronicles 21:12 and no other verse in 2 Chronicles. That is a word search, not a reading of the book. These checked verses do not explicitly settle when the writing was made or how it was delivered. A separate published record deals with the two dates for Jehoram of Israel in 2 Kings 1:17 and 3:1; this record is about the writing. title: “The words of Necho from the mouth of God” — how did a word of God come to the king of Egypt?
summary: Necho of Egypt tells Josiah that God has commanded him to make haste and warns him not to meddle with God. The narrator then says Josiah “hearkened not unto the words of Necho from the mouth of God”. The verses do not say how the command reached Necho, or by what sign Josiah could have known whose word it was.
text: KJV 2 Chronicles 35:20: “Necho king of Egypt came up to fight against Charchemish by Euphrates: and Josiah went out against him” KJV 35:21: “But he sent ambassadors to him, saying, What have I to do with thee, thou king of Judah? I come not against thee this day, but against the house wherewith I have war: for God commanded me to make haste: forbear thee from meddling with God, who is with me, that he destroy thee not.” KJV 35:22: “Nevertheless Josiah would not turn his face from him, but disguised himself, that he might fight with him, and hearkened not unto the words of Necho from the mouth of God, and came to fight in the valley of Megiddo.” KJV 2 Kings 23:29: “and king Josiah went against him; and he slew him at Megiddo, when he had seen him” Hebrew (WLC) 35:21: וֵאלֹהִ֖ים אָמַ֣ר לְבַֽהֲלֵ֑נִי חֲדַל־לְךָ֛ מֵאֱלֹהִ֥ים אֲשֶׁר־עִמִּ֖י וְאַל־יַשְׁחִיתֶֽךָ [and God said to hasten me; cease from God who is with me, and let him not destroy you]. 35:22: וְלֹ֥א שָׁמַ֛ע אֶל־דִּבְרֵ֥י נְכֹ֖ו מִפִּ֣י אֱלֹהִ֑ים [and he did not listen to the words of Necho from the mouth of God]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 35:21: καὶ ὁ Θεὸς εἶπε τοῦ κατασπεῦσαι με· πρόσεχε ἀπὸ τοῦ Θεοῦ τοῦ μετʼ ἐμοῦ, μὴ καταφθείρῃ σε [and God said to hasten me; beware of the God who is with me, lest he destroy you]. 35:22: καὶ οὐκ ἤκουσε τῶν λόγων Νεχαὼ διὰ στόματος Θεοῦ [and he did not listen to the words of Nechao through the mouth of God]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/14/35/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/2CH35.htm.
reasoning: In verse 21 the claim to speak for God is Necho’s own. In verse 22 it is the narrator who says the words were from the mouth of God, and the account of Josiah’s death follows at once. The means matters to how the passage is read: the verses name no prophet, dream or sign by which the command came to Necho, and none by which Josiah was to tell it from the claim of a foreign king.

What the verses do state is that Necho sent ambassadors, what he said, that Josiah did not turn back, and that the narrator calls the words “from the mouth of God”. The Hebrew and the Greek quoted say the same as the KJV on this point. Check made: 35:20–22 were read in the KJV, the Hebrew and Brenton’s Greek, and 2 Kings 23:29 in the KJV; that Kings verse reports no message from Necho. title: “Put the holy ark in the house which Solomon … did build” — where had the ark been?
summary: In Josiah’s eighteenth year the king tells the Levites to put the holy ark in the house Solomon built, and that it shall no longer be a burden on their shoulders. Chronicles had the priests bring the ark into that house at its dedication. The verses checked do not say that the ark had left the house, or where it was when Josiah spoke.

title: “The whole congregation together was forty and two thousand three hundred and threescore” — the counts given add up to far fewer
summary: Ezra and Nehemiah both give 42,360 as the whole congregation. The counts each book lists before that total add up to 29,818 in Ezra and 31,089 in Nehemiah. Neither list reaches the total, and the two sums differ from each other.

title: Who laid the foundation of the house: Sheshbazzar, or Zerubbabel?
summary: The elders’ answer reported in Tatnai’s letter says that Sheshbazzar came and laid the foundation of the house of God. title: The foundation of the temple: laid in the second year of the return, or on the day Haggai names in the second year of Darius?
summary: Ezra says the builders laid the foundation of the temple in the second year after the return, and that the work then stopped until the second year of Darius. title: “Some of them had wives by whom they had children” — what became of the wives and the children?
summary: The book proposes a covenant to put away the foreign wives “and such as are born of them”, reports an inquiry that finished on a stated day, records a pledge by the priests first named, lists the men, and ends by saying that some had children by these wives. title: Between Joiada and Jaddua: Jonathan in one list, Johanan in the other
summary: Nehemiah 12:10–11 gives the line Eliashib, Joiada, Jonathan, Jaddua. title: Chisleu “in the twentieth year”, then Nisan “in the twentieth year of Artaxerxes” — how is the year counted, and whose year is the first?
summary: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. Nehemiah hears the report from Jerusalem in the month Chisleu “in the twentieth year” and speaks to the king in the month Nisan “in the twentieth year of Artaxerxes”. Elsewhere the KJV calls Chisleu the ninth month and Nisan the first. The book does not say from what point its years are counted, or whose twentieth year 1:1 means.

And it came to pass in the month Chisleu, in the twentieth year, as I was in Shushan the palace,” KJV Nehemiah 2:1: “And it came to pass in the month Nisan, in the twentieth year of Artaxerxes the king, that wine was before him” KJV Zechariah 7:1: “in the fourth day of the ninth month, even in Chisleu” KJV Esther 3:7: “In the first month, that is, the month Nisan, in the twelfth year of king Ahasuerus” KJV Nehemiah 5:14: “from the twentieth year even unto the two and thirtieth year of Artaxerxes the king, that is, twelve years” Hebrew (WLC) 1:1: וַיְהִ֤י בְחֹֽדֶשׁ־[כִּסְלֵו כ] (כִּסְלֵיו֙ ק) שְׁנַ֣ת עֶשְׂרִ֔ים [and it came to pass in the month Chislev, year twenty; the bracketed forms are the edition’s written and read spellings of the month]; 2:1: וַיְהִ֣י ׀ בְּחֹ֣דֶשׁ נִיסָ֗ן שְׁנַ֥ת עֶשְׂרִ֛ים לְאַרְתַּחְשַׁ֥סְתְּא הַמֶּ֖לֶךְ [and it came to pass in the month Nisan, year twenty of Artaxerxes the king]. title: “The wall of Jerusalem also is broken down, and the gates thereof are burned with fire” — which breaking and burning is reported to Nehemiah?

title: “Who had been carried away from Jerusalem … with Jeconiah” — Mordecai, or his forefather Kish?
summary: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. The KJV names Mordecai “the son of Jair, the son of Shimei, the son of Kish” and goes on, “Who had been carried away from Jerusalem” with king Jeconiah. The verse does not say whether “who” is Mordecai or the last man named, Kish. The answer decides whether Mordecai himself came from Jerusalem, and so how long before the king’s seventh and twelfth years that carrying away lay.
text: KJV Esther 2:5: “Now in Shushan the palace there was a certain Jew, whose name was Mordecai, the son of Jair, the son of Shimei, the son of Kish, a Benjamite;” KJV Esther 2:6: “Who had been carried away from Jerusalem with the captivity which had been carried away with Jeconiah king of Judah, whom Nebuchadnezzar the king of Babylon had carried away.” KJV 2 Kings 24:15: “And he carried away Jehoiachin to Babylon” KJV Jeremiah 24:1: “after that Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon had carried away captive Jeconiah the son of Jehoiakim king of Judah” KJV Esther 2:16: “in the seventh year of his reign” KJV Esther 3:7: “in the twelfth year of king Ahasuerus” Hebrew (WLC) 2:5: וּשְׁמֹ֣ו מָרְדֳּכַ֗י בֶּ֣ן יָאִ֧יר בֶּן־שִׁמְעִ֛י בֶּן־קִ֖ישׁ אִ֥ישׁ יְמִינִֽי [and his name Mordecai, son of Jair, son of Shimei, son of Kish, a Benjamite]; 2:6: אֲשֶׁ֤ר הָגְלָה֙ מִיר֣וּשָׁלַ֔יִם עִם־הַגֹּלָה֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר הָגְלְתָ֔ה עִ֖ם יְכָנְיָ֣ה מֶֽלֶךְ־יְהוּדָ֑ה [who was carried away from Jerusalem with the captivity that was carried away with Jeconiah king of Judah]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 2:6: ὃς ἦν αἰχμάλωτος ἐξ Ἱερουσαλὴμ, ἣν ᾐχμαλώτευσε Ναβουχοδονόσορ βασιλεὺς Βαβυλῶνος. [who was a captive from Jerusalem, which Nabuchodonosor king of Babylon took captive]. In a passage the KJV does not have, the verse labelled 1:1c says of Mardochaeus: Ἦν δὲ ἐκ τῆς αἰχμαλωσίας, ἦς ᾐχμαλώτευσε Ναβουχοδονόσορ βασιλεὺς Βαβυλῶνος ἐξ Ἰερουσαλὴμ, μετὰ Ἰεχονίου τοῦ βασιλέως τῆς Ἰουδαίας. [and he was of the captivity which Nabuchodonosor king of Babylon took captive from Jerusalem, with Jechonias the king of Judaea]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/17/2/, https://ebible.org/grcbrent/ESG02.htm and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/ESG01.htm.
reasoning: The clause opens with a relative word that follows three forefathers’ names. Read of Mordecai, it makes him a man who was himself taken from Jerusalem in Jeconiah’s day and who is still active in the twelfth year of Ahasuerus. Read of Kish, it dates the family’s removal and says nothing of Mordecai’s age. The verses quoted do not say how many years lie between Jeconiah’s captivity and the reign of Ahasuerus, so the weight of the question depends on which king is meant as well.
scope: Readings, none stated in the two KJV verses: that “who” is Mordecai; that “who” is Kish, the nearest name; or that it speaks of the family as a whole. The Hebrew relative word and the Greek of 2:6 leave the same choice open. The Greek’s added verse 1:1c does state one reading, that Mordecai himself was of that captivity; the KJV and the Hebrew edition have no such verse. A whole-word search of the packaged KJV finds “Jeconiah” at 1 Chronicles 3:16 and 3:17, Esther 2:6 and Jeremiah 24:1, 27:20, 28:4 and 29:2; none of those verses names Mordecai or Kish. title: “But Mordecai bowed not, nor did him reverence” — why not?
summary: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. The king commands that all bow to Haman, and Mordecai does not. He is asked why and no answer of his is reported; the passage says only that “he had told them that he was a Jew”. Haman’s plan to destroy all the Jews follows from this refusal, and the KJV does not state its reason.
text: KJV Esther 3:2: “And all the king's servants, that were in the king's gate, bowed, and reverenced Haman: for the king had so commanded concerning him. But Mordecai bowed not, nor did him reverence.” KJV Esther 3:3: “Why transgressest thou the king's commandment?” KJV Esther 3:4: “when they spake daily unto him, and he hearkened not unto them, that they told Haman, to see whether Mordecai's matters would stand: for he had told them that he was a Jew” KJV Esther 3:5: “when Haman saw that Mordecai bowed not, nor did him reverence, then was Haman full of wrath” KJV Esther 3:6: “wherefore Haman sought to destroy all the Jews that were throughout the whole kingdom of Ahasuerus” Bowing to men elsewhere in the KJV: Genesis 23:7 “And Abraham stood up, and bowed himself to the people of the land”; 1 Samuel 24:8 “David stooped with his face to the earth, and bowed himself” Hebrew (WLC) 3:2: וּמָ֨רְדֳּכַ֔י לֹ֥א יִכְרַ֖ע וְלֹ֥א יִֽשְׁתַּחֲוֶֽה [but Mordecai would not kneel and would not bow down]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 3:2: ὁ δὲ Μαρδοχαῖος οὐ προσεκύνει αὐτῷ. [but Mardochaeus did not do him obeisance]. In a prayer of Mardochaeus that the KJV does not have, the verses labelled 4:17d and 4:17e give a reason: ὅτι οὐκ ἐν ὕβρει, οὐδὲ ἐν ὑπερηφανείᾳ, οὐδὲ ἐν φιλοδοξίᾳ ἐποίησα τοῦτο, τὸ μὴ προσκυνεῖν τὸν ὑπερήφανον Ἀμάν. [that not in insolence, nor in pride, nor in love of glory did I do this, not to do obeisance to the proud Aman] Ἀλλʼ ἐποίησα τοῦτο, ἵνα μὴ θῶ δόξαν ἀνθρώπου ὑπεράνω δόξης Θεοῦ [but I did this that I might not set the glory of a man above the glory of God]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/17/3/, https://ebible.org/grcbrent/ESG03.htm and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/ESG04.htm.
reasoning: Everything that follows in the book turns on this refusal, yet the KJV reports the question put to Mordecai and not his reply. The one clue, that he had told them he was a Jew, is given as the reason the servants informed Haman; it is not said to be the reason he would not bow. In the two other verses quoted, Abraham and David bow to men and the verses record no blame.
scope: Readings, none stated in the KJV verses quoted: that he held bowing to Haman to be forbidden to a Jew; that the refusal was aimed at Haman in particular, for his descent or his person; or that it was a matter between the two men which the book does not tell. The Greek’s added prayer states one reason, that he would not set a man’s glory above God’s; the KJV and the Hebrew edition have no such passage. Genesis 23:7 and 1 Samuel 24:8 were chosen as examples of bowing to men; other passages on bowing were not collected, and the kind of bowing Haman was to receive is not described. title: “Enlargement and deliverance … from another place” — from where, and why would Esther’s house still be destroyed?
summary: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. Mordecai tells Esther that if she keeps silent, deliverance will come to the Jews “from another place”, but she and her father’s house will be destroyed. He does not say what the other place is, on what he rests his certainty, or by whom her house would be destroyed if the Jews are delivered.
text: KJV Esther 4:13: “Think not with thyself that thou shalt escape in the king's house, more than all the Jews” KJV Esther 4:14: “For if thou altogether holdest thy peace at this time, then shall there enlargement and deliverance arise to the Jews from another place; but thou and thy father's house shall be destroyed: and who knoweth whether thou art come to the kingdom for such a time as this?” KJV Esther 4:16: “fast ye for me, and neither eat nor drink three days, night or day” Hebrew (WLC) 4:14: רֶ֣וַח וְהַצָּלָ֞ה יַעֲמֹ֤וד לַיְּהוּדִים֙ מִמָּקֹ֣ום אַחֵ֔ר וְאַ֥תְּ וּבֵית־אָבִ֖יךְ תֹּאבֵ֑דוּ [relief and deliverance will arise for the Jews from another place, and thou and thy father’s house will perish]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 4:14: ἄλλοθεν βοήθεια καὶ σκέπη ἔσται τοῖς Ἰουδαίοις· σὺ δὲ καὶ ὁ οἶκος τοῦ πατρός σου ἀπολεῖσθε [from elsewhere help and shelter will be for the Jews; but thou and thy father’s house will perish]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/17/4/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/ESG04.htm.
reasoning: The sentence is the turning point of Esther’s decision, and it rests on an assurance whose ground is not given. If “another place” means God, the verse does not say so; if it means some other human helper, none is named. The second half is as open: the verse does not say whether Esther’s house would fall amid violence from which other Jews were delivered, or by a judgment on her silence. The promise of deliverance does not itself specify that every threatened person survives.
scope: Readings, none stated in the verses quoted: that “another place” is a guarded way of speaking of God; that it means another person or power at court; or that Mordecai speaks from confidence in earlier promises to his people, which he does not cite. The Hebrew and the Greek are as general as the KJV here. A whole-word search of the packaged KJV of Esther finds neither “God” nor “Lord” in the book; the Greek names the Lord at 4:8, in words the KJV does not have, and that difference is set out in another record. The fast of 4:16 names no one to whom it is addressed. This is not presented as a contradiction or as a fault in the passage. title: Job’s wife: one sentence in the KJV, a speech of six lines in the Greek
summary: In the KJV, with the Hebrew, Job’s wife says one sentence. Brenton’s Greek says that much time had passed and gives her a longer speech about her dead children, Job sitting in the open air among worms, and her own life as a wandering servant.

title: Satan “came also among them” — is he one of the sons of God, and by what standing does he come before the Lord?
summary: Twice Satan comes before the Lord with the sons of God, is questioned, and is given power over Job within limits. The passage does not say whether he is one of the sons of God, what his office is, or why he is admitted.

Then Satan answered the Lord, and said, From going to and fro in the earth, and from walking up and down in it.” KJV 1:12: “Behold, all that he hath is in thy power; only upon himself put not forth thine hand. So Satan went forth from the presence of the Lord.” KJV 2:1: “and Satan came also among them to present himself before the Lord” KJV 2:6: “And the Lord said unto Satan, Behold, he is in thine hand; but save his life.” KJV 2:7: “So went Satan forth from the presence of the Lord, and smote Job with sore boils” Other places where the KJV Old Testament has the name: 1 Chronicles 21:1: “And Satan stood up against Israel, and provoked David to number Israel.” Psalms 109:6: “and let Satan stand at his right hand” Zechariah 3:1: “and Satan standing at his right hand to resist him” Zechariah 3:2: “The Lord rebuke thee, O Satan” KJV Revelation 12:10: “for the accuser of our brethren is cast down, which accused them before our God day and night” Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/18/1/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/JOB01.htm.
reasoning: The verses quoted state what Satan does: he comes on the day the sons of God come, says he has been going to and fro in the earth, challenges the Lord about Job, is twice given leave with a limit, and goes out from the presence of the Lord. title: “There was a man in the land of Uz” — where was Uz, and when did Job live?
summary: The book opens with a man in the land of Uz, the greatest of the men of the east. The opening names no king, no year, no father and no people for him. Brenton’s Greek adds a passage at the end of the book that gives a place, a line of descent and another name; the Hebrew and the KJV have no such passage.
text: KJV Job 1:1: “There was a man in the land of Uz, whose name was Job; and that man was perfect and upright, and one that feared God, and eschewed evil.” Hebrew (WLC) 1:1: אִ֛ישׁ הָיָ֥ה בְאֶֽרֶץ־ע֖וּץ אִיֹּ֣וב שְׁמֹ֑ו. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 1:1: ἌΝΘΡΩΠΟΣ τις ἦν ἐν χώρᾳ τῇ Αὐσίτιδι, ᾧ ὄνομα Ἰὼβ. KJV 1:3: “so that this man was the greatest of all the men of the east” The name Uz elsewhere in the KJV. Genesis 10:23: “And the children of Aram; Uz, and Hul, and Gether, and Mash.” Genesis 36:28: “The children of Dishan are these; Uz, and Aran.” Jeremiah 25:20: “and all the kings of the land of Uz” Lamentations 4:21: “O daughter of Edom, that dwellest in the land of Uz” Job named elsewhere. Ezekiel 14:14: “Though these three men, Noah, Daniel, and Job, were in it” James 5:11: “Ye have heard of the patience of Job” The end of the book. KJV Job 42:17: “So Job died, being old and full of days.” Brenton’s Greek prints 42:17 and then five lettered verses, 17a to 17e, which the Hebrew edition and the KJV do not have. 17b: Οὗτος ἑρμηνεύεται ἐκ τῆς Συριακῆς βίβλου, ἐν μὲν γῇ κατοικῶν τῇ Αὐσίτιδι, ἐπὶ τοῖς ὁρίοις τῆς Ἰδουμαίας καὶ Ἀραβίας· προϋπῆρχε δὲ αὐτῷ ὄνομα Ἰωβάβ· [This man is interpreted out of the Syriac book as dwelling in the land of Ausitis, on the borders of Idumaea and Arabia; and his name before was Jobab]. 17c, in part: ὥστε εἶναι αὐτὸν πέμπτον ἀπὸ Ἁβραάμ· [so that he was the fifth from Abraam]. KJV Genesis 36:33 has a Jobab among the kings of Edom: “Jobab the son of Zerah of Bozrah reigned in his stead” Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/18/1/, https://ebible.org/grcbrent/JOB01.htm and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/JOB42.htm.
reasoning: In the KJV and the Hebrew the opening places Job by one name of a land and by the phrase “the men of the east”, and gives no reign, generation or kindred by which to date him. The other KJV verses that have the name Uz use it of a son of Aram, of a son of Dishan, of a land with kings (Jeremiah), and of a land where the daughter of Edom dwells (Lamentations); none of them mentions Job. Where and when Job lived bears on how his sacrifices, his knowledge of God and the book’s relation to Israel are read.

title: “A messenger with him, an interpreter, one among a thousand” — the Greek has a thousand death-bearing angels
summary: In the KJV, with the Hebrew, Elihu speaks of one messenger, an interpreter, one among a thousand, who shews a man his uprightness. Brenton’s Greek speaks of a thousand death-bearing angels, none of whom shall wound the man.
text: KJV Job 33:23: “If there be a messenger with him, an interpreter, one among a thousand, to shew unto man his uprightness:” Hebrew (WLC) 33:23: אִם־יֵ֤שׁ עָלָ֨יו ׀ מַלְאָ֗ךְ מֵלִ֗יץ אֶחָ֥ד מִנִּי־אָ֑לֶף לְהַגִּ֖יד לְאָדָ֣ם יָשְׁרֹֽו. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 33:23, first two clauses, as printed: Ἐὰν ὦσι χιλιοι αγγελοι θανατηφόροι, εἷς αὐτῶν οὐ μὴ τρώσῃ αὐτόν· [If there be a thousand death-bearing angels, not one of them shall wound him;] The same Greek verse goes on: ἐὰν νοήσῃ τῇ καρδίᾳ ἐπιστραφῆναι πρὸς Κύριον, ἀναγγείλῃ δὲ ἀνθρώπῳ τὴν ἑαυτοῦ μέμψιν, τὴν δὲ ἄνοιαν αὐτοῦ δείξῃ, [if he purpose in his heart to turn to the Lord, and declare to man his own fault, and shew his folly,] KJV Job 33:24: “Then he is gracious unto him, and saith, Deliver him from going down to the pit: I have found a ransom.” Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/18/33/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/JOB33.htm.
reasoning: In the KJV the thousand is the number out of which one messenger comes, and what is shewn to man is “his uprightness”. In the Greek the thousand are themselves the angels, they are called death-bearing, and what is declared to man is “his own fault” and “his folly”.
scope: G applies at 33:23. Only this verse was compared in the Greek; the Greek of 33:24 was not compared with the KJV here. title: “Canst thou draw out leviathan with an hook?” — the Greek has “a dragon”

title: “Ye have not spoken of me the thing which is right, like my servant Job” — the Greek of 42:8 has “against my servant Job”, and 42:9 has their sin pardoned
summary: In the KJV, with the Hebrew, the Lord twice tells the friends that they have not spoken of him what is right, as Job has. Brenton’s Greek keeps that at 42:7 but at 42:8 says they have not spoken truth against Job, adds that the Lord would have destroyed them but for Job, and at 42:9 says he pardoned their sin because of Job where the KJV says the Lord accepted Job.
text: KJV Job 42:7: “for ye have not spoken of me the thing that is right, as my servant Job hath” Brenton Greek 42:7: οὐ γὰρ ἐλαλήσατε ἐνώπιόν μου ἀληθὲς οὐδὲν, ὥσπερ ὁ θεράπων μου Ἰώβ. [for ye have spoken before me nothing true, as my servant Job has.] KJV Job 42:8: “lest I deal with you after your folly, in that ye have not spoken of me the thing which is right, like my servant Job” Hebrew (WLC) 42:8: כִּ֠י לֹ֣א דִבַּרְתֶּ֥ם אֵלַ֛י נְכֹונָ֖ה כְּעַבְדִּ֥י אִיֹּֽוב; the same seven words stand in the Hebrew of 42:7: כִּ֠י לֹ֣א דִבַּרְתֶּ֥ם אֵלַ֛י נְכֹונָ֖ה כְּעַבְדִּ֥י אִיֹּֽוב. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 42:8: εἰ μὴ γὰρ διʼ αὐτὸν, ἀπώλεσα ἂν ὑμᾶς· οὐ γὰρ ἐλαλήσατε ἀληθὲς κατὰ τοῦ θεράποντός μου Ἰώβ. [for but for him I would have destroyed you; for ye have not spoken truth against my servant Job.] KJV Job 42:9: “the Lord also accepted Job” Hebrew (WLC) 42:9: וַיִּשָּׂ֥א יְהוָ֖ה אֶת־פְּנֵ֥י אִיֹּֽוב. Brenton Greek 42:9: καὶ ἔλυσε τὴν ἁμαρτίαν αὐτοῖς διὰ Ἰὼβ. [and he loosed their sin for them because of Job.] Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/18/42/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/JOB42.htm.
reasoning: At 42:8 the KJV makes the friends’ fault their words about the Lord and makes Job the pattern of right speech. The Greek of that verse makes Job the one their untrue words were against, and names destruction as what they were spared. At 42:9 the KJV reports what the Lord did for Job; the Greek reports what he did for the friends.

title: Elihu speaks from chapter 32 to chapter 37 — why does the Lord’s verdict name Job and three friends and not him?
summary: Elihu is first named at Job 32:2, angry with Job and with the three friends, and speaks through chapter 37. When the Lord gives his verdict he names Eliphaz and his “two friends” and Job. The verses quoted do not say whether Elihu spoke rightly, or why he is not named.
text: KJV Job 2:11 names those who came: “Now when Job's three friends heard of all this evil that was come upon him, they came every one from his own place; Eliphaz the Temanite, and Bildad the Shuhite, and Zophar the Naamathite” KJV Job 32:2: “Then was kindled the wrath of Elihu the son of Barachel the Buzite, of the kindred of Ram: against Job was his wrath kindled, because he justified himself rather than God.” KJV 32:3: “Also against his three friends was his wrath kindled, because they had found no answer, and yet had condemned Job.” KJV 32:4: “Now Elihu had waited till Job had spoken, because they were elder than he.” After Elihu’s last words, KJV 38:1: “Then the Lord answered Job out of the whirlwind, and said,” KJV 38:2: “Who is this that darkeneth counsel by words without knowledge?” Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 38:1: Μετὰ δὲ τὸ παύσασθαι Ἐλιοὺν τῆς λέξεως, εἶπεν ὁ Κύριος τῷ Ἰὼβ διὰ λαίλαπος καὶ νεφῶν, [And after Elius had ceased from his speech, the Lord said to Job through whirlwind and clouds,] KJV 42:7: “And it was so, that after the Lord had spoken these words unto Job, the Lord said to Eliphaz the Temanite, My wrath is kindled against thee, and against thy two friends: for ye have not spoken of me the thing that is right, as my servant Job hath.” KJV 42:9: “So Eliphaz the Temanite and Bildad the Shuhite and Zophar the Naamathite went, and did according as the Lord commanded them” Fetched from https://ebible.org/grcbrent/JOB38.htm.
reasoning: The narrator says Elihu was angry with both sides. Elihu is introduced as speaker at 32:6, 34:1 and 35:1 and again at 36:1, and a search of the packaged KJV of chapters 32–37 for a line that introduces a speaker (“answered … and said”, “spake … and said”, “proceeded, and said”) finds those four verses only. The Lord’s verdict at 42:7 sorts the speakers into those who did not speak rightly (Eliphaz and his two friends) and Job. Elihu is in neither group as named. Whether his speeches are approved, condemned or passed over changes how chapters 32–37 are to be read: as a true answer to Job, as one more mistaken speech, or as something the verdict does not address.

Each is an interpretation; the verses quoted state none of them, in the KJV or in the Greek quoted, and this record asserts none. title: “Ye have not spoken of me the thing that is right, as my servant Job hath” — which words of Job are meant?
summary: The Lord tells Eliphaz that Job has spoken of him what is right. Shortly before, the Lord has asked who darkens counsel by words without knowledge and whether Job will condemn him, and Job has said that he uttered what he did not understand. The verse does not say which of Job’s words were right.
text: KJV Job 42:7: “And it was so, that after the Lord had spoken these words unto Job, the Lord said to Eliphaz the Temanite, My wrath is kindled against thee, and against thy two friends: for ye have not spoken of me the thing that is right, as my servant Job hath.” KJV 42:8 repeats it: “in that ye have not spoken of me the thing which is right, like my servant Job” The Lord to Job. KJV 38:2: “Who is this that darkeneth counsel by words without knowledge?” KJV 40:2: “Shall he that contendeth with the Almighty instruct him? he that reproveth God, let him answer it.” KJV 40:8: “Wilt thou also disannul my judgment? wilt thou condemn me, that thou mayest be righteous?” Job to the Lord. KJV 40:4: “Behold, I am vile; what shall I answer thee? I will lay mine hand upon my mouth.” KJV 42:3: “Who is he that hideth counsel without knowledge? therefore have I uttered that I understood not; things too wonderful for me, which I knew not.” KJV 42:6: “Wherefore I abhor myself, and repent in dust and ashes.”
reasoning: Within five chapters the Lord both challenges Job’s words (38:2, 40:2, 40:8) and holds up Job’s speech as right against the friends’ (42:7, 42:8), and Job himself says that he uttered what he did not understand (42:3) and that he repents (42:6). The verdict names no speech. Which words it approves decides how Job’s long complaints in the dialogue are to be read: as right speech about God, or as the words without knowledge that the Lord challenged.
scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. Possible readings: that the right words are Job’s last answers (40:4–5 and 42:2–6); that they are his speeches as a whole, set against what the friends said of God; and that the verdict is about speaking to the Lord and not about what was said of him. Each is an interpretation; the verses quoted state none of them, and this record asserts none. The two sets of verses need not conflict: a speaker can be right in one thing and without knowledge in another, and the passage does not say that this is how they fit. A separate record compares the Greek of 42:7–9; the Greek of 42:7 quoted there has “as my servant Job” and names no speech either, and the Greek of 42:8 is worded differently. A published record on 42:7 notes that the book corrects its own speakers; it does not ask which of Job’s words are approved. Check made: Job 38:1–3, 40:1–8 and 42:1–9 were read in the packaged KJV; Job’s speeches in chapters 3–31 were not re-read for this record, and no other book was searched. This record quotes the packaged KJV only; the separate Greek comparison is described as context.

title: Behemoth and leviathan — what creatures does the Lord point Job to?
summary: The Lord’s speech from the whirlwind (40:6) sets two creatures before Job, behemoth and leviathan, and describes each at length. The KJV keeps both words as names. The verses quoted do not say what kind of creature either one is.
text: KJV Job 40:15: “Behold now behemoth, which I made with thee; he eateth grass as an ox.” KJV 40:17: “He moveth his tail like a cedar” KJV 40:23: “Behold, he drinketh up a river, and hasteth not” KJV Job 41:1: “Canst thou draw out leviathan with an hook? or his tongue with a cord which thou lettest down?” KJV 41:19: “Out of his mouth go burning lamps, and sparks of fire leap out.” KJV 41:21: “His breath kindleth coals, and a flame goeth out of his mouth.” KJV 41:34: “He beholdeth all high things: he is a king over all the children of pride.” The name leviathan elsewhere in the KJV. Psalms 74:14: “Thou brakest the heads of leviathan in pieces” Psalms 104:26: “There go the ships: there is that leviathan, whom thou hast made to play therein.” Isaiah 27:1: “shall punish leviathan the piercing serpent, even leviathan that crooked serpent; and he shall slay the dragon that is in the sea” Hebrew (WLC) 40:15: הִנֵּה־נָ֣א בְ֭הֵמֹות. Hebrew (WLC) for KJV 41:1, numbered 40:25 in that edition: תִּמְשֹׁ֣ךְ לִוְיָתָ֣ן בְּחַכָּ֑ה. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/18/40/.
reasoning: The speech uses the two creatures to answer Job, so what they are bears on what the answer is. The description joins things said of a grazing animal and a creature of the water (grass, a river, a hook) with things that go beyond that (a flame from the mouth, heads in the plural in the psalm, a kingship over “all the children of pride”). If they are animals Job could see, the speech can be read as pointing to God’s rule over the made world; if they are creatures of another kind, it can be read as pointing to powers beyond ordinary animals. The text names them and does not say which.
scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. Possible readings: that they are two known animals described in heightened language; that they are animals no longer known; and that they are creatures of a kind other than ordinary animals, as Isaiah 27:1 speaks of leviathan beside “the dragon that is in the sea”. Each is an interpretation; the verses quoted state none of them, in the KJV or in the Hebrew quoted, and this record asserts none. The speech is in verse, and this record does not test its pictures against natural history. A shared name in the Psalms and Isaiah does not settle that the same creature is meant in Job. Two separate records compare the Greek, which has “beasts” at 40:15 and a common noun for a dragon or serpent at KJV 41:1; the Greek verses quoted in those records keep neither name. summary: The KJV says God “is angry with the wicked every day”. Brenton’s Greek describes the daily expression of wrath differently: God is a righteous judge, strong and patient, “not” bringing wrath every day.

title: “Thy throne, O God, is for ever and ever” — who is the king of Psalm 45, and who is called “God”?

title: Who speaks the curses of Psalm 109:6–19: is it the psalmist’s own prayer, or words he reports from his adversaries?
summary: Psalm 109 first speaks of adversaries in the plural (“they”), then of a single man (“him”, “he”) in a series of curses, then of “mine adversaries” again. The verses quoted do not say whether the curses are the psalmist’s own words or words he reports from his adversaries.
text: KJV Psalms 109:2: “For the mouth of the wicked and the mouth of the deceitful are opened against me: they have spoken against me with a lying tongue.” KJV Psalms 109:4–5: “For my love they are my adversaries: but I give myself unto prayer.” “And they have rewarded me evil for good, and hatred for my love.” KJV Psalms 109:6–8: “Set thou a wicked man over him: and let Satan stand at his right hand.” “When he shall be judged, let him be condemned: and let his prayer become sin.” “Let his days be few; and let another take his office.” KJV Psalms 109:16–19: “Because that he remembered not to shew mercy, but persecuted the poor and needy man, that he might even slay the broken in heart.” “As he loved cursing, so let it come unto him: as he delighted not in blessing, so let it be far from him.” “As he clothed himself with cursing like as with his garment, so let it come into his bowels like water, and like oil into his bones.” “Let it be unto him as the garment which covereth him, and for a girdle wherewith he is girded continually.” KJV Psalms 109:20–21: “Let this be the reward of mine adversaries from the Lord, and of them that speak evil against my soul.” “But do thou for me, O God the Lord, for thy name's sake: because thy mercy is good, deliver thou me.”
reasoning: In the verses quoted, 109:2–5 speak of what “they” have done to the speaker. From 109:6 the verbs and pronouns of the verses quoted are about a single person, “him” and “he”, and the verses quoted from 109:6 to 109:19 are wishes for harm to that person or statements of why it is wished. At 109:20 the speaker refers to “mine adversaries” and to “them that speak evil against my soul”, and at 109:21 turns to ask the Lord to do something for him. The verses quoted do not mark where the curses begin or end as someone’s reported speech, and do not say who the single man of 109:6–19 is. Possible readings: (1) the curses are the psalmist’s own prayer against one adversary among those named in the plural; (2) the curses are the words the adversaries spoke against the psalmist, which he reports before 109:20 answers them; (3) the plural adversaries and the single man are the same people spoken of in two numbers. The record does not decide between them.
