title: “Ye waters that be above the heavens” — which waters does Psalm 148:4 call on to praise?
summary: Psalm 148:4 calls on “ye heavens of heavens, and ye waters that be above the heavens” to praise the Lord. The verses quoted do not say which waters these are, where they are, or whether they are the waters that Genesis 1:7 places above the firmament.
text: KJV Psalms 148:3–4: “Praise ye him, sun and moon: praise him, all ye stars of light.” “Praise him, ye heavens of heavens, and ye waters that be above the heavens.” KJV Psalms 148:5–6: “Let them praise the name of the Lord: for he commanded, and they were created.” “He hath also stablished them for ever and ever: he hath made a decree which shall not pass.” KJV Genesis 1:6–8: “And God said, Let there be a firmament in the midst of the waters, and let it divide the waters from the waters.” “And God made the firmament, and divided the waters which were under the firmament from the waters which were above the firmament: and it was so.” “And God called the firmament Heaven. And the evening and the morning were the second day.”
reasoning: Psalm 148:4 names two things after “Praise him”: “ye heavens of heavens” and “ye waters that be above the heavens”. Psalm 148:5–6 say of “them” that they were created at the Lord’s command and established for ever by a decree. The verses quoted do not say which waters are above the heavens, where the heavens are, or what separates the two. Genesis 1:7 speaks of “the waters which were above the firmament” and Genesis 1:8 calls the firmament “Heaven”, so a reader may take the psalm to speak of the same waters. Possible readings: (1) the waters of Genesis 1:6–7, with the “heavens” of the psalm as the firmament Genesis 1:8 calls Heaven; (2) waters the psalm names without reference to Genesis; (3) a call to praise that names a part of creation without saying what it is. The record does not decide between them.
scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. The question is limited to the verses quoted. The record does not examine other passages about waters above the heavens, does not say that any reading is the right one, and does not set the psalm against Genesis or against any account of the sky. The published records on the Genesis firmament are separate and are not examined here.

title: “He that winneth souls is wise” — the Greek has “the souls of transgressors are cut off before their time”
summary: The KJV of Proverbs 11:30 ends “he that winneth souls is wise”. Brenton’s Greek ends with a clause that Brenton’s English renders “the souls of transgressors are cut off before their time”.
text: KJV Proverbs 11:30: “The fruit of the righteous is a tree of life; and he that winneth souls is wise.” Hebrew (WLC) 11:30: וְלֹקֵ֖חַ נְפָשֹׂ֣ות חָכָֽם. Brenton’s Greek 11:30: ἀφαιροῦνται δὲ ἄωροι ψυχαὶ παρανόμων. Brenton’s own English (https://ebible.org/eng-Brenton/PRO11.htm) prints: “but the souls of transgressors are cut off before their time”. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/20/11/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/PRO11.htm.
reasoning: Both texts end the verse with a clause about “souls”. In the KJV the person is one who “winneth” souls and is called wise. title: “Since the days of Jeshua the son of Nun unto that day had not the children of Israel done so” — yet the feast of tabernacles is reported kept before
summary: Nehemiah 8 says that when the returned congregation made booths and sat under them, the children of Israel had not done so since the days of Joshua. text: KJV Isaiah 7:10–14: “Moreover the Lord spake again unto Ahaz, saying,” “Ask thee a sign of the Lord thy God; ask it either in the depth, or in the height above.” “But Ahaz said, I will not ask, neither will I tempt the Lord.” “And he said, Hear ye now, O house of David; Is it a small thing for you to weary men, but will ye weary my God also?” “Therefore the Lord himself shall give you a sign; Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel.” KJV Isaiah 7:15–16: “Butter and honey shall he eat, that he may know to refuse the evil, and choose the good.” “For before the child shall know to refuse the evil, and choose the good, the land that thou abhorrest shall be forsaken of both her kings.” KJV Isaiah 8:3–4: “And I went unto the prophetess; and she conceived, and bare a son. Then said the Lord to me, Call his name Mahershalalhashbaz.” “For before the child shall have knowledge to cry, My father, and my mother, the riches of Damascus and the spoil of Samaria shall be taken away before the king of Assyria.” KJV Isaiah 8:8: “And he shall pass through Judah; he shall overflow and go over, he shall reach even to the neck; and the stretching out of his wings shall fill the breadth of thy land, O Immanuel.” KJV Isaiah 8:10: “Take counsel together, and it shall come to nought; speak the word, and it shall not stand: for God is with us.” KJV Isaiah 8:18: “Behold, I and the children whom the Lord hath given me are for signs and for wonders in Israel from the Lord of hosts, which dwelleth in mount Zion.” A search of the packaged KJV text of Isaiah 1–27 for “virgin” finds 7:14, 23:4 and 23:12 (23:4 and 23:12 are not about this sign); for “Immanuel” it finds 7:14 and 8:8.
reasoning: The sign is given to “you”, the house of David (7:13–14); verse 16 says that before “the child” knows to refuse the evil “the land that thou abhorrest shall be forsaken of both her kings”. The verses name no mother and no father, and give no year. In chapter 8 the prophet goes to “the prophetess”, who conceives and bears a son named Mahershalalhashbaz, and verse 4 gives a similar timing (“before the child shall have knowledge to cry, My father, and my mother”); verse 8 addresses “O Immanuel”, and verse 18 says the prophet and “the children whom the Lord hath given me” are signs. Possible readings: a child born in the time of Ahaz to a woman of the court or of the prophet’s household, whom the text does not name; the child of 8:3–4 under another name; or a child still future from Ahaz’s time. The record does not decide between them.

title: “The land shadowing with wings, which is beyond the rivers of Ethiopia” — which land is meant?
summary: Isaiah 18:1 addresses “the land shadowing with wings, which is beyond the rivers of Ethiopia”. The verses quoted do not name the land that is addressed.
text: KJV Isaiah 18:1–2: “Woe to the land shadowing with wings, which is beyond the rivers of Ethiopia:” “That sendeth ambassadors by the sea, even in vessels of bulrushes upon the waters, saying, Go, ye swift messengers, to a nation scattered and peeled, to a people terrible from their beginning hitherto; a nation meted out and trodden down, whose land the rivers have spoiled!” KJV Isaiah 18:7: “In that time shall the present be brought unto the Lord of hosts of a people scattered and peeled, and from a people terrible from their beginning hitherto; a nation meted out and trodden under foot, whose land the rivers have spoiled, to the place of the name of the Lord of hosts, the mount Zion.” KJV Isaiah 13:1: “The burden of Babylon”; 15:1: “The burden of Moab”; 17:1: “The burden of Damascus”; 19:1: “The burden of Egypt”; 23:1: “The burden of Tyre”. A search of the packaged KJV text of Isaiah 1–27 for “shadowing with wings” finds 18:1 only.
reasoning: Other burdens in these chapters name their subject in the opening line: Babylon (13:1), Moab (15:1), Damascus (17:1), Egypt (19:1) and Tyre (23:1). Chapter 18 begins with a description and a position, “beyond the rivers of Ethiopia”, and not with a name. The people are sent ambassadors “by the sea” (18:2) and a present is brought “to the place of the name of the Lord of hosts, the mount Zion” (18:7). Possible readings: a land south of Egypt that the verse describes by the rivers of Ethiopia; Ethiopia itself; or a people that the verse describes by a position and a description and not by a name. The record does not decide between them.

title: “Watchman, what of the night?” — who calls, who answers, and what are the morning and the night?
summary: Isaiah 21:11–12 has a voice call “out of Seir” to the watchman, and the watchman answers “The morning cometh, and also the night”. The verses quoted do not say who calls, what the morning and the night are, or what the invitation to “enquire” leads to.
text: KJV Isaiah 21:6: “For thus hath the Lord said unto me, Go, set a watchman, let him declare what he seeth.” KJV Isaiah 21:11–12: “The burden of Dumah. He calleth to me out of Seir, Watchman, what of the night? Watchman, what of the night?” “The watchman said, The morning cometh, and also the night: if ye will enquire, enquire ye: return, come.” A search of the packaged KJV text of Isaiah 1–27 for “Dumah” finds 21:11 only, and for “Seir” 21:11 only.
reasoning: The verse is headed “The burden of Dumah”, and the call comes “out of Seir”; 21:6 also tells the prophet to set a watchman, but these quotations do not establish that the two watchmen are the same. The verses do not say who “he” is who calls to the prophet, whether the question is asked for Dumah or for Seir, or what the morning and the night stand for: relief followed by trouble, a change of rule, or two events the verse leaves unnamed. The watchman’s reply also invites a further enquiry (“if ye will enquire, enquire ye: return, come”), which the verses do not carry on. Possible readings: a call from Edom to the prophet for news of the night’s end; a call to the watchman of the prophet’s own people from a land that is not his; or a call from Seir whose speaker the verses leave unnamed. The record does not decide between them.

text: KJV Jeremiah 3:16: “And it shall come to pass, when ye be multiplied and increased in the land, in those days, saith the Lord, they shall say no more, The ark of the covenant of the Lord: neither shall it come to mind: neither shall they remember it; neither shall they visit it; neither shall that be done any more.” KJV 2 Chronicles 35:3: “And said unto the Levites that taught all Israel, which were holy unto the Lord, Put the holy ark in the house which Solomon the son of David king of Israel did build; it shall not be a burden upon your shoulders: serve now the Lord your God, and his people Israel,”
reasoning: The verse says what will no longer be said, thought of, remembered, visited or done, and puts it in the future, in the days when the people are “multiplied and increased in the land”. It does not say whether the ark is then gone, kept, or replaced. “Neither shall that be done any more” does not say what “that” is: making the ark, visiting it, or the saying. 2 Chronicles 35:3 puts the ark “in the house which Solomon … did build”. Possible readings: the ark is lost or taken; the ark is set aside; the saying is only dropped. The record does not decide between them.
scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. The question is limited to the two verses quoted. The record does not say that any reading is the right one, does not rest on the Hebrew or the Greek, and does not claim that no other passage says more about the ark.

title: “These nations shall serve the king of Babylon seventy years” — from what event are the seventy years counted?
summary: Jeremiah 25:11 says the nations “shall serve the king of Babylon seventy years” and 29:10 says “after seventy years be accomplished at Babylon I will visit you”. The verses quoted do not say what event begins the count.
text: KJV Jeremiah 25:11: “And this whole land shall be a desolation, and an astonishment; and these nations shall serve the king of Babylon seventy years.” KJV Jeremiah 25:12: “And it shall come to pass, when seventy years are accomplished, that I will punish the king of Babylon, and that nation, saith the Lord, for their iniquity, and the land of the Chaldeans, and will make it perpetual desolations.” KJV Jeremiah 29:10: “For thus saith the Lord, That after seventy years be accomplished at Babylon I will visit you, and perform my good word toward you, in causing you to return to this place.” KJV 2 Chronicles 36:21: “To fulfil the word of the Lord by the mouth of Jeremiah, until the land had enjoyed her sabbaths: for as long as she lay desolate she kept sabbath, to fulfil threescore and ten years.”
reasoning: Jeremiah 25:11 gives a length of time and a service, and 25:12 says what happens “when seventy years are accomplished”. title: “the third year of the reign of Jehoiakim … came Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon” or “the fourth year of Jehoiakim … the first year of Nebuchadrezzar”?
summary: Daniel 1:1 has Nebuchadnezzar, “king of Babylon”, come against Jerusalem “in the third year of the reign of Jehoiakim”. Jeremiah 25:1 says the fourth year of Jehoiakim “was the first year of Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon”. Jeremiah 46:2 puts his smiting of Pharaohnecho in that fourth year.
text: KJV Daniel 1:1: “In the third year of the reign of Jehoiakim king of Judah came Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon unto Jerusalem”. KJV Jeremiah 25:1: “in the fourth year of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah king of Judah, that was the first year of Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon”. KJV Jeremiah 46:2: “Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon smote in the fourth year of Jehoiakim”.
reasoning: Daniel 1:1 names Nebuchadnezzar “king of Babylon” in the third year of Jehoiakim. Jeremiah 25:1 gives the fourth year of Jehoiakim as the first year of Nebuchadrezzar, and 46:2 gives that fourth year for the battle at Carchemish. Read as worded, the king is called king of Babylon one year before his first year. The two statements could both stand if the two books count the years of a reign by different methods, or if the title in Daniel 1:1 is the title used of him when the event is told; neither passage says how the years are counted.
scope: No tag is proposed: the record compares the wording of the KJV only, and does not rest on the Hebrew or the Greek. It does not say that either book is mistaken, and it does not say that the siege of Daniel 1:1 and the battle of Jeremiah 46:2 are the same event. The spellings Nebuchadnezzar and Nebuchadrezzar are the KJV’s two spellings of the name and are not the point.

title: “Beat your plowshares into swords” or “they shall beat their swords into plowshares”?
summary: Joel 3:10 has the nations told “Beat your plowshares into swords and your pruninghooks into spears”. Micah 4:3 and Isaiah 2:4 have the same two pairs of tools in the opposite direction: swords into plowshares and spears into pruninghooks.
text: KJV Joel 3:10: “Beat your plowshares into swords and your pruninghooks into spears”. KJV Micah 4:3: “they shall beat their swords into plowshares, and their spears into pruninghooks”. KJV Isaiah 2:4: “they shall beat their swords into plowshares, and their spears into pruninghooks”.
reasoning: The same two pairs of things, plowshares with swords and pruninghooks with spears, are changed in one direction in Joel and in the other in Micah and Isaiah. Read as worded, the verses describe opposite transformations of the same tools in different settings; Joel gives a command, while Micah and Isaiah describe future conduct. The verses could both stand: Joel 3:9–10 is spoken to the nations as a call to prepare war, and Micah 4:3 and Isaiah 2:4 describe the nations’ conduct when the Lord has judged among them; neither passage refers to the other.
scope: No tag is proposed: the record compares the wording of the KJV only, and does not rest on the Hebrew or the Greek. It does not say that either passage is mistaken, does not say that the passages are one saying or two, and does not say which of the writers had the other’s words in view. Isaiah 2:4 is given as the third verse of the same wording; the pair at issue is Joel 3:10 against Micah 4:3.

title: “the northern army” — who or what is it?
summary: Joel 2:20 has the Lord promise to “remove far off from you the northern army”. Joel 1:6 describes “a nation … come up upon my land”, and 2:25 names the cankerworm, caterpiller, palmerworm and locust as “my great army which I sent among you”. The verses do not say whether the northern army is the same as these.
text: KJV Joel 2:20: “I will remove far off from you the northern army”. KJV Joel 1:6: “a nation is come up upon my land, strong, and without number”. KJV Joel 2:25: “my great army which I sent among you”. KJV Joel 2:11: “the Lord shall utter his voice before his army”.
reasoning: The northern army is not named, and the verse that names it gives a direction, north, and a fate, driven into a barren land, with “his stink” going up. The passage also calls the locust and its kin “my great army” at 2:25 and uses “army” of the Lord’s host at 2:11. It does not say that the northern army is the locust, a human army, or the Lord’s host. Possible readings, named only as readings: the swarm of insects of chapter 1, described by direction; a human army from the north; a figure of the day of the Lord. The record does not decide between them.
scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. The question is limited to the verses quoted. The record does not say that any reading is the right one, does not rest on the Hebrew or the Greek, and does not claim that no other passage says more. The published entry on locust and army imagery (the entry exp-late-28-2-4), which compares Joel 2:4 and 2:25 and does not ask who the northern army is.
